items.title: Calculating the Radius of Gyration of a Uniform Rectangular Laminar

key_prerequisites.name: Moments of Inertia of Laminas About the Coordinate Axes

sections.normalized_html: A rectangular plate of mass [MATH: M] and uniform mass density occupies the region [MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.] Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the [MATH: y]-axis.
sections.readable_text:
A rectangular plate of mass [MATH: M] and uniform mass density occupies the region
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.] Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the [MATH: y]-axis.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region [MATH: D] with mass [MATH: M] and mass density function [MATH: \lambda(x,y),] we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by [MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},] where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: x]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by [MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},] where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] about the origin is given by [MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},] where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis is defined as

[MATH: I_y = \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm{d}A,]

where [MATH: \lambda(x,y)] is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate [MATH: D] is [MATH: \mathcal{A} = 3\cdot 1 = 3.] Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by [MATH: \lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{M}{3}.]

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis is

[MATH: I_{y}|= ∬_(D)x^{2}λ(x, y)dA; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}∫_{0}^{3}x^{2}dxdy; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}[(1)/(3)x^{3}]_{0}^{3}dy; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}9dy; = 3M∫_{1}^{2}dy; = 3M[y]_{1}^{2}; = 3M(2 − 1); = 3M.]

Finally,

[MATH: R_y^2 =\dfrac{3M}{M} = 3\quad \Rightarrow\quad R_y = \sqrt{3}.]

sections.normalized_html: A plate of mass [MATH: M] occupies the region [MATH: D] bounded by the lines [MATH: y = x,] [MATH: x = 1,] and the [MATH: x]-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by [MATH: \lambda(x,y) = 3Mx.] Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.
sections.readable_text: A plate of mass [MATH: M] occupies the region [MATH: D] bounded by the lines [MATH: y = x,] [MATH: x = 1,] and the [MATH: x]-axis. Its mass density at any point on the plate is given by [MATH: \lambda(x,y) = 3Mx.] Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the origin.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region [MATH: D] with mass [MATH: M] and mass density function [MATH: \lambda(x,y),] we have the following definitions:

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by [MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},] where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: x]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by [MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},] where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] about the origin is given by [MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},] where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as [MATH: I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2 + y^2) \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A,] where [MATH: \lambda(x,y)] is the mass density function. The region [MATH: D] is a type I region with representation [MATH: D = \left\{(x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq x \right\}.]

Hence, the moment of inertia about the origin is [MATH: I_{0}|= ∬_(D)(x^{2} + y^{2})λ(x, y)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{x}(x^{2} + y^{2}) ⋅ 3Mxdydx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{x}x^{3} + xy^{2}dydx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}[x^{3}y + (1)/(3)xy^{3}]_{y = 0}^{y = x}dx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}x^{4} + (1)/(3)x^{4}dx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}(4)/(3)x^{4}dx; = 3M[(4)/(15)x^{5}]_{0}^{1}; = 3M ⋅ (4)/(15); = (4M)/(5).]

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the origin is [MATH: R_{0}|= sqrt((I_{0})/(M)); = sqrt((4M)/(5) ⋅ (1)/(M)); = sqrt((4)/(5)); = (2)/(sqrt(5)); = (2sqrt(5))/(5).]

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by [MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},] where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: x]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by [MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},] where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis.

  • The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] about the origin is given by [MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},] where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia about the origin.

In polar coordinates, the region occupied by the plate is given by [MATH: D = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}.]

The moment of inertia about the origin, in polar coordinates, is defined as

[MATH: I_0 = \iint\limits_D \lambda(r,\theta) r^3 \:\textrm{d}r\:\textrm{d}\theta,]

where [MATH: \lambda(r,\theta)] is the mass density function.

Also, the mass density in terms of polar coordinates is [MATH: \lambda(r,\theta)=\dfrac{3}{2}Mr\sin\theta.] Therefore, the moment of inertia about the origin is

[MATH: I_{0}|= ∬_(D)λ(r, θ)r^{3}drdθ; = (3)/(2)M∫_{0}^{π}∫_{0}^{1}r^{4}\sin θdrdθ; = (3)/(2)M(∫_{0}^{1}r^{4}dr)(∫_{0}^{π}\sin θdθ); = (3)/(2)M ⋅ (1)/(5)r^{5}|_{0}^{1} ⋅ (− \cos θ)|_{0}^{π}; = (3)/(2)M ⋅ (1)/(5) ⋅ 2; = (3M)/(5).]

[MATH: R_{0}|= sqrt((I_{0})/(M)); = sqrt((3M)/(5) ⋅ (1)/(M)); = sqrt((3)/(5)).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In this lesson, we discuss a concept analogous to center of mass that applies to rotating bodies.

Content:
Recall that the center of mass of a plane lamina is defined as the point [MATH: (\bar{x},\bar{y})] in the coordinate plane where the entire mass of the lamina could be concentrated to produce the same total moment about the coordinate axes as the original laminar.

Content:
Analogously, the radius of gyration of a plane lamina is the distance [MATH: R] from an axis of rotation [MATH: L] that the entire mass [MATH: M] of the lamina would need to be concentrated to produce the same moment of inertia as the original lamina.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/d99e2d8e363d0fff68a16bc593c1c95e]

Content:
To derive an explicit formula for the radius of gyration, recall that the moment of inertia of a particle [MATH: P] of mass [MATH: m] at a distance of [MATH: r] from an axis of rotation equals

Content:
[MATH: mr^2.]

Content:
So, for a particle of mass [MATH: M] at a distance of [MATH: R] from the axis of rotation [MATH: L,] the moment of inertia about [MATH: L] is given by
[MATH: MR^2.]

Content:
The radius of gyration is defined as the distance [MATH: R] that a particle of mass [MATH: M] must be placed to give the same moment of inertia as the original lamina. Therefore, it is the solution to the equation

Content:
[MATH: I = MR^2,]

Content:
where [MATH: I] is the moment of inertia of the lamina about [MATH: L.]

Content:
Rearranging this equation, we find that the radius of gyration is given by
[MATH: R = \sqrt{\dfrac{I}{M}}.]

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: A Summary of Key Results

Content:
In this lesson, we'll limit the axis of rotation to the [MATH: x]-axis, the [MATH: y]-axis, and the origin. We summarize the key results below:

Content:
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] of a lamina about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by [MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},] where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia of the lamina about the [MATH: x]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] of a lamina about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by [MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},] where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia of the lamina about the [MATH: y]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] of a lamina about the origin is given by [MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},] where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia of the lamina about the origin.

Item 3 — Example: Calculating the Radius of Gyration of a Uniform Rectangular Laminar

Example Prompt:
A rectangular plate of mass [MATH: M] and uniform mass density occupies the region
[MATH: D = \big\{ (x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 3, \:\: 1 \leq y \leq 2 \big\}.] Find the radius of gyration of the plate about the [MATH: y]-axis.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region [MATH: D] with mass [MATH: M] and mass density function [MATH: \lambda(x,y),] we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by
[MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: x]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by
[MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] about the origin is given by
[MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis is defined as

[MATH: I_y = \iint\limits_D x^2\lambda(x,y) \:\textrm{d}A,]

where [MATH: \lambda(x,y)] is the mass density function.

The area of the rectangular plate [MATH: D] is [MATH: \mathcal{A} = 3\cdot 1 = 3.] Since the plate has uniform density, the mass density function is given by
[MATH: \lambda(x,y) = \dfrac{M}{\mathcal{A}} = \dfrac{M}{3}.]

Therefore, the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis is

[MATH: I_{y}|= ∬_(D)x^{2}λ(x, y)dA; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}∫_{0}^{3}x^{2}dxdy; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}[(1)/(3)x^{3}]_{0}^{3}dy; = (M)/(3)∫_{1}^{2}9dy; = 3M∫_{1}^{2}dy; = 3M[y]_{1}^{2}; = 3M(2 − 1); = 3M.]

Finally,

[MATH: R_y^2 =\dfrac{3M}{M} = 3\quad \Rightarrow\quad R_y = \sqrt{3}.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
For a plane lamina in the shape of a region [MATH: D] with mass [MATH: M] and mass density function [MATH: \lambda(x,y),] we have the following definitions:

- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_x] about the [MATH: x]-axis is given by
[MATH: R_x = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_x}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_x] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: x]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_y] about the [MATH: y]-axis is given by
[MATH: R_y = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_y}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_y] is the moment of inertia about the [MATH: y]-axis.
- The radius of gyration [MATH: R_0] about the origin is given by
[MATH: R_0 = \sqrt{\dfrac{I_0}{M}},]
where [MATH: I_0] is the moment of inertia about the origin.

The moment of inertia about the origin is defined as
[MATH: I_0 = \iint\limits_D (x^2 + y^2) \lambda(x,y) \: \textrm{d}A,]
where [MATH: \lambda(x,y)] is the mass density function. The region [MATH: D] is a type I region with representation
[MATH: D = \left\{(x,y) \: : \: 0 \leq x \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq y \leq x \right\}.]

Hence, the moment of inertia about the origin is
[MATH: I_{0}|= ∬_(D)(x^{2} + y^{2})λ(x, y)dA; = ∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{x}(x^{2} + y^{2}) ⋅ 3Mxdydx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}∫_{0}^{x}x^{3} + xy^{2}dydx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}[x^{3}y + (1)/(3)xy^{3}]_{y = 0}^{y = x}dx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}x^{4} + (1)/(3)x^{4}dx; = 3M∫_{0}^{1}(4)/(3)x^{4}dx; = 3M[(4)/(15)x^{5}]_{0}^{1}; = 3M ⋅ (4)/(15); = (4M)/(5).]

Therefore, the radius of gyration about the origin is
[MATH: R_{0}|= sqrt((I_{0})/(M)); = sqrt((4M)/(5) ⋅ (1)/(M)); = sqrt((4)/(5)); = (2)/(sqrt(5)); = (2sqrt(5))/(5).]
